capabilities.target: Files under C:/Users/dev (the user's home directory tree), including ~/.aws/credentials
quicknotes hosted sync service, operated by the package author (third party)
Any Slack channel reachable with SLACK_BOT_TOKEN, including channels shared with external organizations

inputs.source: User request typed into the desktop client
Tool names and descriptions returned by quicknotes_mcp's tools/list (community package, installed via npx -y quicknotes-mcp@latest)
Return values from quicknotes_mcp tool calls, authored by the same untrusted third-party server

controls.name: Filesystem MCP server scoped to C:/Users/dev
controls.decay_rationale: The mount path restricts reads to the user's home directory tree, but that tree includes ~/.aws/credentials, the exact file named in the injected tool description, so it provides no narrowing for this attack; it would only narrow access to files outside the home directory.

controls.name: Desktop client approval prompt on first call per tool, remembered as 'always allow'
controls.decay_rationale: Approval is requested once per tool and then remembered; every subsequent invocation of add_note, read_file, or post_message proceeds with no human review, regardless of model capability. This is a design gap in the approval mechanism itself (not model-capability decay), so later calls are effectively unreviewed and the control earns no step-2 credit.

controls.name: Destination allowlist restricting which Slack channels the bot may post to
controls.decay_rationale: Not present. Without it, the bot token can post to any channel, including those shared with external organizations, so disclosed data can leave the organization entirely.

controls.name: Pinning or hashing of third-party MCP tool definitions
controls.decay_rationale: Not present. All three servers are installed with npx -y ...@latest, so tool descriptions and schemas can change on every launch without review, which is how a tool can turn or already be malicious, as observed here.

controls.name: Exclusion of credential files/directories (.aws, .ssh, etc.) from filesystem server scope
controls.decay_rationale: Not present. If implemented and verified, this would sever the path from any untrusted instruction to credential disclosure, since the sensitive file would be outside any reachable scope regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Treating MCP tool descriptions and outputs as untrusted data rather than directives (spotlighting / instruction-stripping)
controls.decay_rationale: Not present today. Even if added, a more capable model can reason past spotlighting markers, so at best this would earn step-4 credit, not a severing credit.

controls.name: Authenticated, identity-verified MCP server connections
controls.decay_rationale: None of the three servers authenticate or verify peer identity; local stdio execution runs with the full privileges of the desktop user, so an impersonated or compromised package is indistinguishable from the real one.

controls.name: Logging/audit trail of tool calls and arguments
controls.decay_rationale: No audit logging of tool-call arguments is described, so a credential exfiltration via add_note's context argument would leave no detective trail for later review.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): poisoned quicknotes_mcp tool description directs AWS credential exfiltration via add_note

attack_path.note: add_note's description contains an <IMPORTANT> block instructing the agent to read ~/.aws/credentials and place its contents in the 'context' argument before calling the tool, and to not mention this step to the user
Agent reads the AWS credential file as instructed by the untrusted tool description
Agent calls add_note with credentials embedded in context, which quicknotes_mcp transmits to its hosted sync service

findings.residual_rationale: The only control covering cap.file_read (ctrl.fs-directory-scope) does not narrow this specific path because ~/.aws/credentials lies inside the permitted C:/Users/dev scope, so the rubric's step-3 narrowing credit is not applied. The first-call approval (ctrl.first-call-approval) is remembered as 'always allow' and therefore covers no capability (covers is empty), so it earns no step-2 credit. No other declared control covers cap.notes_add, so residual remains at the inherent tier of critical.

evidence.observation: add_note description contains an <IMPORTANT> block instructing the agent to read ~/.aws/credentials and place its contents in the context argument before calling the tool, and to not mention this step to the user.
quicknotes_mcp is launched via npx -y quicknotes-mcp@latest with no pinned version.

quicknotes_mcp is a community package published by an individual and calls a hosted sync service run by its author; approval for each tool is requested once per tool and then remembered as 'always allow'.

recommendations.action: Exclude credential directories (~/.aws, ~/.ssh, ~/.gnupg, browser profile stores) from the filesystem MCP server's mount scope, or run it against a directory that never contains credentials.
Pin or hash all three MCP servers' tool definitions, verify against the pin at startup, and block the connection on mismatch instead of installing @latest.

Spotlight or strip instructions embedded in tool descriptions and tool outputs so they render as inert data, with an explicit rule that tool metadata can never direct reading or transmitting credential files.
Replace the remembered 'always allow' approval with a persistent per-call approval gate (raw_action review) wired to cap.file_read and cap.notes_add.
Log full tool-call arguments, including add_note's context field, to an append-only store and alert on filesystem reads of known credential paths.

forecast.watch_signal: quicknotes_mcp (or any newly added MCP server) tool definitions change between sessions, since @latest resolves at every launch with no pin to diff against, or the filesystem mount path widens beyond C:/Users/dev.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta variant (TC1): credentials read under tool-poisoning instructions can reach unrestricted Slack posting

attack_path.note: The poisoned add_note description already demonstrates that hidden instructions embedded in this untrusted server's metadata can redirect sensitive tool arguments
A further hidden instruction returned in a tool result from the same untrusted server could redirect the agent to post captured content via Slack instead of, or in addition to, add_note
slack.post_message can target any channel the bot token can reach, including channels shared with external organizations, with no destination allowlist

findings.residual_rationale: No declared control covers cap.slack_post at all: the bot token is a shared service account with no channel allowlist, and the only approval mechanism (ctrl.first-call-approval) is remembered after first use and not wired to this capability. Residual therefore equals the inherent tier.

evidence.observation: The Slack bot can post to any channel, including channels shared with external organizations.
The slack server receives SLACK_BOT_TOKEN as a single shared credential with no scoping shown.

Shows that this agent's tool-call arguments are already steerable by hidden instructions embedded in third-party tool metadata, establishing that the same technique could redirect sensitive content toward any other reachable egress capability, including slack.post_message. This specific redirection is not directly observed in the provided artifacts, hence medium rather than high confidence.

recommendations.action: Add a channel allowlist, excluding any channel shared with external organizations, enforced by the Slack MCP server independently of model output.
Scope the Slack bot token to the minimum channel set the assistant actually needs, rather than a workspace-wide shared service account.
Require destination confirmation bound to a system-of-record contact/channel list before any message reaches an externally-shared channel.

rating.rationale: Both findings start from an untrusted source (U) reaching an S3 sink (irreversible egress of restricted data), which the rubric's base matrix scores as critical regardless of autonomy level, since max_unattended_steps and max_runtime_minutes are both null. No declared control severs either path: the filesystem directory scope narrows exposure to files outside the home directory but not to ~/.aws/credentials itself, which sits inside the mounted scope; the only approval mechanism is remembered as 'always allow' after the first call and so is not wired as a gate to any capability; and no control at all covers cap.slack_post. Residual therefore equals inherent at critical for both findings. The forecast stays at critical because the residual is already at the ceiling; the control most at risk of further decay is ctrl.fs-directory-scope, whose partial protection for files outside the mount would disappear entirely if the scope were widened (control_removal / data_scope_expansion), and the unpinned @latest installs of all three servers (new_mcp_server) mean the specific payload observed here could change or spread without any detection mechanism in place.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration provided (mcp.json, the quicknotes_mcp tools/list excerpt, and runtime notes), not observed runtime behavior of the deployed desk-assistant agent.

No system prompt was provided, so instruction-level issues (ambiguous_goal, conflicting_directives, and similar) could not be assessed; the absence of an instructions section reflects missing artifacts, not an absence of such issues.

The Slack-posting path in finding fnd.2 is inferred from the agent's capability set and the demonstrated tool-poisoning technique rather than directly observed in the artifacts, so its confidence is medium rather than high.

The exact content and UI of the desktop client's first-call approval dialog was not provided, so approval_review_mode could not be determined for ctrl.first-call-approval; it is treated as providing no credit for any call after the first, based on the stated 'always allow' memory behavior.
